justification: Structurally this is a strong article: a clean H2 outline with four purposeful H3s under 'What depth-first search is actually for', a TOC that reads as a table of contents of the argument, restrained and well-placed callouts (:::dotnet, :::pitfall), and four exercises spaced through the piece with varied forms (predict-before-running, adapt-the-algorithm, find-the-bug, prove-the-theorem, extend-the-counter) whose solutions are correctly collapsed behind 'Show solution' and never spoil the visible output. Both figures are genuinely informative rather than decorative -- Figure 1's three-level BFS fan-out and Figure 2's DFS tree with a non-tree-edge legend both have correct <title>/<desc>, remap color classes cleanly between light and dark, hold no overflow at 390 px in either theme, and their captions say exactly what to notice (Figure 1: why Cache has no level-2 child; Figure 2: why the legend edges are not back edges). No GFM tables are used, so there is no table-clipping risk, and mobileOverflowPx is 0 site-wide. Two real problems keep it off the pass bar. First, Lighthouse performance is 86, a genuine fail against the binding >=90 gate on every category, driven by an unusually heavy single HTML document (418 of 422 KiB) served uncompressed in the verify server -- FCP/LCP both land at 3.3s. Total byte weight this high for a text-only article is itself worth a look: the same eight-entry 'modules' dictionary literal is retyped in full in at least nine separate code blocks across the piece, which is good for run-code self-containment but adds real, avoidable HTML weight. Second, and specific to this article's content, the BFS/DFS visit-order comparisons that are the entire subject of the piece are printed with `string.Join(" ", ...)` over eight node names, producing output lines of 55-70 characters; at the 390 px/40-column budget the back half of the list -- the very thing being compared -- disappears under the fade in at least five code blocks (the opening traverse example, the queue-for-stack skeleton, exercise 1's solution, the topological-sort output, and the recursive-vs-stack-forward-vs-stack-reversed comparison). The worst instance is the 'What both cost' edge-count table, where the entire 'DFS edges' column -- the numeric proof that DFS examines exactly as many edges as BFS -- is cut off completely on a phone, not just its tail; a reader has to infer the value by symmetry with the visible 'edges' and 'BFS edges' columns rather than read it. Two of the five join-output clippings are substantially mitigated because the prose spells the same node lists out in full as wrapped inline code (the DfsIterative-vs-Dfs comparison, and rooms/hallway which is short enough to fit anyway); the topo-sort order and the recursive/stack comparison are not restated and stay genuinely lost on mobile. Against the GeeksforGeeks BFS page this is still clearly better: no borrowed C-style pseudocode split across four languages, one running example instead of a new toy each time, and worked exercises with solutions instead of none. Against Sedgewick & Wayne's own site, this article covers strictly more ground (cycle detection, topological sort, components, and the iterative-DFS edge-classification pitfall all in one place) with runnable, checked C# throughout.

issues.problem: At 390 px the entire 'DFS edges' column is off-screen, not merely faded -- the table cuts after 'BFS edges' in the header and after the BFS-edges value in every data row. This is the one place in the article that turns the O(V+E) claim into a number a reader can check, and the DFS half of that check is invisible on the majority-share device.

Verify against a mobile screenshot after the change.
